stem: Which of the following best represents the typical stages of the data lifecycle?

options.text: Create, store, use, share, archive, destroy
options.rationale: The data lifecycle commonly spans creation, storage, use, sharing, archival, and destruction — each stage needing appropriate controls.

options.text: Boot, run, sleep, shutdown
options.rationale: Those are system power states, not data lifecycle stages.

options.text: Buy, sell, trade, lease
options.rationale: These are commercial transactions, unrelated to the data lifecycle.

options.text: Encrypt, decrypt, re-encrypt
options.rationale: These are cryptographic operations, not lifecycle stages.

stem: An organization applies different controls when data is stored versus when it is shared externally. This MOST directly reflects which lifecycle concept?

options.text: Security controls should be tailored to each stage of the data lifecycle
options.rationale: Different lifecycle stages present different risks, so controls (e.g., at-rest encryption vs sharing agreements) are tailored per stage.

options.text: All lifecycle stages require identical controls
options.rationale: Uniform controls ignore the differing risks at each stage.

options.text: Data has no lifecycle
options.rationale: Data clearly moves through lifecycle stages, each with distinct handling needs.

options.text: Only destruction needs any controls
options.rationale: Every stage — creation through destruction — requires appropriate controls.

stem: At which point in the data lifecycle should classification ideally FIRST occur?

options.text: At creation, so appropriate controls apply from the start
options.rationale: Classifying data at creation ensures the correct handling and protection controls are applied throughout its entire lifecycle.

options.text: Only at destruction
options.rationale: Classifying only at destruction leaves the data unprotected for its entire useful life.

options.text: Never; classification is optional
options.rationale: Classification drives protection and is not optional for sensitive data.

options.text: Only after a breach
options.rationale: Waiting until a breach means the data was unclassified and under-protected when it mattered.

stem: Data no longer used daily but required for compliance is moved to long-term storage. During this archival stage, what is BEST maintained?

options.text: Protection appropriate to its classification, plus retrievability for its required retention period
options.rationale: Archived data must remain protected per its sensitivity and retrievable for as long as retention/compliance requires.

options.text: Immediate deletion regardless of retention rules
options.rationale: Deleting data still under a retention requirement could violate legal/compliance obligations.

options.text: Public exposure to save storage costs
options.rationale: Exposing archived sensitive data publicly is a serious confidentiality failure.

options.text: Removal of all encryption to speed access
options.rationale: Stripping protection from archived sensitive data increases risk.

stem: When data reaches the end of its lifecycle and is no longer needed or required to be retained, what is the MOST appropriate action?

options.text: Securely destroy it using a method appropriate to its sensitivity and media type
options.rationale: End-of-life data should be securely destroyed (per its sensitivity/media) to prevent later unauthorized recovery, once no retention obligation remains.

options.text: Keep it forever just in case
options.rationale: Indefinite retention of unneeded data increases risk and storage/compliance burden.

options.text: Leave it on decommissioned drives in a closet
options.rationale: Retaining sensitive data on forgotten media is a common breach source.

options.text: Sell the media without sanitization
options.rationale: Selling media with recoverable data causes data leakage.

stem: A company collects far more personal data than it uses, increasing breach exposure. Which lifecycle principle BEST addresses this?

options.text: Data minimization — collect and retain only what is necessary
options.rationale: Minimization reduces the amount of data held, shrinking breach impact and compliance scope across the lifecycle.

options.text: Collect as much data as possible for future use
options.rationale: Maximizing collection increases exposure and contradicts minimization.

options.text: Never delete any data
options.rationale: Retaining everything indefinitely enlarges the attack surface and violates minimization.

options.text: Duplicate all data across many systems
options.rationale: Widespread duplication increases exposure rather than minimizing it.

stem: During the 'share' stage, sensitive data is sent to an external partner. Which control is MOST important?

options.text: Ensure a data-sharing agreement and secure transmission govern the exchange
options.rationale: Sharing sensitive data externally requires both contractual governance (agreement) and secure transmission to protect it.

options.text: Send it over an unencrypted public channel
options.rationale: Unencrypted external transmission exposes the data to interception.

options.text: Share without recording who received it
options.rationale: Failing to track recipients removes accountability and traceability.

options.text: Post it publicly for convenience
options.rationale: Public posting of sensitive data is a direct confidentiality breach.

stem: An organization securely deletes production copies of sensitive data but forgets that backups still contain it. What lifecycle lesson does this MOST clearly illustrate?

options.text: Lifecycle controls (including destruction) must account for all copies, including backups and archives
options.rationale: Effective destruction and retention management must cover every copy of data — including backups — or sensitive data persists unmanaged.

options.text: Backups are irrelevant to data lifecycle
options.rationale: Backups are copies of the data and are very much part of its lifecycle and destruction scope.

options.text: Only production data ever matters
options.rationale: Backups hold the same sensitive data and must be governed too.

options.text: Deletion of one copy destroys all copies
options.rationale: Deleting one copy does not affect independent backup copies, which is the point of the failure.

stem: To ensure data is properly protected at every lifecycle stage, what is BEST established?

options.text: Clear ownership and accountability for the data throughout its lifecycle
options.rationale: Assigning ongoing ownership ensures someone is accountable for correct handling at each lifecycle stage.

options.text: No owner, so responsibility is shared by no one
options.rationale: Without an owner, no one ensures proper handling and gaps appear.

options.text: Ownership only during creation, then abandonment
options.rationale: Data needs governance across its whole life, not just at creation.

options.text: Transfer ownership to unrelated third parties randomly
options.rationale: Random transfer of ownership breaks accountability.

stem: During the storage stage of the lifecycle, which control MOST directly protects sensitive data confidentiality?

options.text: Encryption of the data at rest
options.rationale: At-rest encryption protects the confidentiality of stored data during the storage lifecycle stage.

options.text: A faster network switch
options.rationale: Network speed does not protect stored data confidentiality.

options.text: A brighter monitor
options.rationale: Display settings are irrelevant to protecting stored data.

options.text: More frequent office cleaning
options.rationale: Cleaning has no bearing on data-at-rest confidentiality.

stem: A company keeps all data indefinitely because 'deleting is scary.' What is the BEST lifecycle-aligned correction?

options.text: Define and enforce retention schedules so data is kept only as long as needed, then securely destroyed
options.rationale: Retention schedules operationalize the lifecycle's end, retaining data only as required and destroying it thereafter to reduce risk.

options.text: Continue keeping everything forever
options.rationale: Indefinite retention increases breach exposure and compliance burden.

options.text: Delete everything immediately without schedules
options.rationale: Indiscriminate deletion could violate legal retention requirements.

options.text: Randomly delete data with no policy
options.rationale: Random deletion risks losing records needed for compliance or operations.

stem: During the 'use' stage, which control MOST directly ensures only authorized personnel access the data?

options.text: Access controls enforcing least privilege and need-to-know
options.rationale: Access controls governing who can use the data enforce least privilege/need-to-know during active use.

options.text: Deleting the data before anyone can use it
options.rationale: Deleting data needed for use defeats its purpose and is not an access control.

options.text: Publishing the data to everyone
options.rationale: Public exposure is the opposite of restricting access to authorized users.

options.text: Disabling all authentication
options.rationale: Removing authentication lets anyone access the data, defeating access control.

stem: An analytics team needs to know where a data set originated and how it was transformed. Tracking this lineage across the lifecycle is BEST described as what?

options.text: Data provenance/lineage
options.rationale: Data provenance/lineage records a data set's origin and transformations, supporting integrity and trust across the lifecycle.

options.text: Data remanence
options.rationale: Remanence is residual data on media, not a record of origin/transformation.

options.text: Data classification
options.rationale: Classification labels sensitivity; it does not track origin and transformations.

options.text: Data encryption
options.rationale: Encryption protects confidentiality; it is not a lineage record.

stem: After a vendor destroys end-of-life media containing sensitive data, what should the organization obtain FIRST for assurance?

options.text: A certificate of destruction documenting what was destroyed and how
options.rationale: A certificate of destruction provides documented assurance that the specific media was destroyed by an appropriate method.

options.text: A verbal 'it's done' with no record
options.rationale: Unrecorded verbal assurance is not verifiable evidence of destruction.

options.text: Nothing; assume it happened
options.rationale: Unverified assumptions leave the organization exposed and non-compliant.

options.text: A marketing flyer from the vendor
options.rationale: Marketing material is not evidence that specific media was destroyed.

stem: Data lifecycle management is best described as which of the following?

options.text: Governing data with appropriate controls from creation through destruction
options.rationale: Lifecycle management applies suitable controls at every stage of data's existence, from creation to secure destruction.

options.text: Only encrypting data once, at creation
options.rationale: It spans all stages, not a single one-time action.

options.text: Deleting data as soon as it is created
options.rationale: Immediate deletion is not lifecycle management and would destroy needed data.

options.text: Ignoring data after it is stored
options.rationale: Lifecycle management continues through use, sharing, archival, and destruction.

stem: When sensitive data is stored with a cloud provider, which lifecycle concern is MOST important to clarify contractually?

options.text: How data is protected, retained, and securely destroyed/returned at end of service
options.rationale: In the cloud, the customer must ensure the provider protects, retains, and securely destroys or returns data appropriately across the lifecycle.

options.text: The provider's office decor
options.rationale: Decor is irrelevant to data lifecycle governance.

options.text: The color of the provider's logo
options.rationale: Branding has no lifecycle relevance.

options.text: The provider's cafeteria menu
options.rationale: This is unrelated to protecting and disposing of data.

stem: As data ages, its sensitivity sometimes decreases (or increases). How should the lifecycle process MOST appropriately handle this?

options.text: Periodically review and reclassify data so controls match current sensitivity
options.rationale: Reclassification during the lifecycle keeps controls aligned with the data's current sensitivity, avoiding over- or under-protection.

options.text: Freeze the original classification forever
options.rationale: Static classification drifts out of alignment with changing sensitivity.

options.text: Delete data whenever its sensitivity changes
options.rationale: Sensitivity change calls for reclassification, not automatic destruction of possibly-needed data.

options.text: Ignore sensitivity changes entirely
options.rationale: Ignoring changes leads to mismatched controls.

stem: At the creation stage, ensuring data is accurate and captured correctly BEST protects which property later in the lifecycle?

options.text: Integrity — accurate data at creation prevents propagating errors downstream
options.rationale: Getting data right at creation preserves integrity throughout the lifecycle, since errors introduced early propagate through use and sharing.

options.text: Availability only
options.rationale: Accuracy at creation primarily concerns integrity, not availability.

options.text: Physical door security
options.rationale: Data-creation accuracy is unrelated to physical door controls.

options.text: Network bandwidth
options.rationale: Bandwidth is unrelated to data accuracy/integrity at creation.

stem: Who holds PRIMARY accountability for ensuring a data set is managed appropriately across its lifecycle?

options.text: The data owner
options.rationale: The data owner is accountable for the data's proper handling and protection across its entire lifecycle.

options.text: The night-shift janitor
options.rationale: This role has no accountability for data governance.

options.text: An anonymous end user
options.rationale: End users use data within granted rights but do not own lifecycle accountability.

options.text: A random external party
options.rationale: External parties do not hold accountability for the organization's data lifecycle.

stem: Which of the following is LEAST relevant to managing the data lifecycle?

options.text: The brand of the employee's office chair
options.rationale: Office furniture branding has no bearing on how data is created, protected, retained, or destroyed, making it least relevant.

options.text: Retention and destruction schedules
options.rationale: Retention/destruction schedules are core lifecycle elements.

options.text: Stage-appropriate protection controls
options.rationale: Applying controls per stage is central to lifecycle management.

options.text: Classification at creation
options.rationale: Classifying at creation drives lifecycle protection and is highly relevant.
